questions.question: Q1. Define instantaneous velocity.
questions.answer: Instantaneous velocity is the velocity at a particular instant, equal to the limit of Δs/Δt as Δt→0, i.e. v = ds/dt.
questions.shortcut: Instantaneous = derivative; average = Δs/Δt.
questions.example: Speedometer reading is instantaneous speed.

questions.question: Q2. Define acceleration. State its SI unit.
questions.answer: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, a = dv/dt. SI unit = m s⁻².
questions.shortcut: a = Δv/Δt (or dv/dt).
questions.example: 0 to 60 m/s in 20 s → a = 3 m/s².

questions.question: Q3. Distinguish uniform and non-uniform acceleration.
questions.answer: Uniform acceleration: equal change in velocity in equal times (a constant). Non-uniform: change varies with time (a not constant), e.g. a body moving in a circle.
questions.shortcut: constant a → uniform; changing a → non-uniform.
questions.example: Free fall = uniform (a=g); car braking = non-uniform.

questions.question: Q4. Find velocity and acceleration for s = 5t − t² at t = 3 s.
questions.answer: v = ds/dt = 5 − 2t → at t=3, v = −1 m/s (1 m/s opposite). a = d²s/dt² = −2 m/s² (constant).
questions.shortcut: v = 1st derivative of s; a = 2nd derivative.
questions.example: Negative v means the particle reverses direction.

questions.question: Q5. What is the significance of the slope of a displacement-time graph?
questions.answer: The slope (gradient) of a s–t graph equals velocity. A steeper slope → larger speed; zero slope → body at rest; negative slope → motion opposite to positive direction. ▥ 3.1 Instantaneous Velocity & Acceleration  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Average vs Instantaneous Velocity & Acceleration ▣ 3.2 Relative Velocity
questions.shortcut: slope of s-t = v; slope of v-t = a.
questions.example: Horizontal s-t line → body stationary.

questions.question: Q6. Define relative velocity of A with respect to B.
questions.answer: Relative velocity of A w.r.t. B is V_AB = V_A − V_B, the velocity at which A appears to move when observed from B.
questions.shortcut: V_AB = V_A − V_B (opposite object first minus reference).
questions.example: Train A 30 m/s, B 20 m/s same line → A w.r.t. B = 10 m/s.

questions.question: Q7. Two trains move in opposite directions at 20 m/s and 30 m/s. Find relative speed.
questions.answer: Opposite directions → add: relative speed = 20 + 30 = 50 m/s.
questions.shortcut: Same direction → subtract; opposite → add.
questions.example: A passenger on the 20 m/s train sees the other at 50 m/s.

questions.question: Q8. A man walks on a moving train. Express his velocity w.r.t. the ground.
questions.answer: If the train's velocity is V and his velocity on the train is u, his ground velocity is V + u (same line, vector sum). ▥ 3.2 Relative Velocity  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Relative Velocity: Standard Situations ▣ 3.3 Equations of Motion
questions.shortcut: Add velocities in same direction; subtract if he walks opposite.
questions.example: Train 15 m/s + man 3 m/s forward = 18 m/s w.r.t. ground.

questions.question: Q9. Derive v = u + at using a v-t graph.
questions.answer: On a v–t graph of uniform acceleration, v = u + (slope)×t, and slope = a. Hence v = u + at.
questions.shortcut: Area under v-t = s; slope = a; final height = u + at.

questions.question: Q10. A body starts from rest and moves 96 m in 8 s with uniform acceleration. Find a.
questions.answer: s = ½at² → 96 = ½·a·64 → a = 3 m/s².
questions.shortcut: From rest: s = ½at², v = at, v² = 2as.

questions.question: Q11. Find the stopping distance of a car at 30 m/s with deceleration 5 m/s².
questions.shortcut: Use v²=u²+2as when time is not given.
questions.example: Hence the minimum safe braking distance is 90 m.

questions.question: Q12. State and derive s = ut + ½at².
questions.answer: s = (average velocity)×t = [(u+v)/2]t = [(u+u+at)/2]t = ut + ½at². ▥ 3.3 Equations of Motion  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Equations of Motion: Which One to Use ▣ 3.4 Freely Falling Body
questions.shortcut: From v=u+at in average-velocity form.

questions.question: Q13. Define a freely falling body and state its acceleration.
questions.answer: A freely falling body is one falling under gravity only, ignoring air resistance. Its acceleration is g ≈ 9.8 m/s² downward, so u=0, a=g.
questions.shortcut: From rest: v = gt, h = ½gt².
questions.example: After 2 s, v = 19.6 m/s, h = 19.6 m.

questions.question: Q14. Time of fall from a 44.1 m height.
questions.example: A stone dropped from a 44.1 m tower hits the ground in 3 s.

questions.question: Q15. Why do all bodies fall with the same acceleration in a vacuum?
questions.answer: In a vacuum there is no air resistance, so the only force is gravity. Since F=mg and a=F/m=g, the mass cancels and every body has the same acceleration g regardless of mass.
questions.shortcut: In vacuum: a = g for all, mass-independent.
questions.example: Feather and coin fall together on the Moon.

questions.question: Q16. Find the height of a tower if a body takes 4 s to fall from its top.
questions.answer: h = ½gt² = ½(9.8)(16) = 78.4 m. ▥ 3.4 Freely Falling Body  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Body Thrown Up vs Down from a Height h ▣ 3.5 Projectile Motion
questions.shortcut: h = ½gt².
questions.example: Tower ≈ 78.4 m tall.

questions.question: Q17. Define projectile motion and state its assumptions.
questions.answer: Projectile motion is the motion of a body thrown into the air under gravity only. Assumptions: neglect air resistance, g constant, motion in a vertical plane, acceleration only vertical.
questions.shortcut: Horizontal: uniform velocity. Vertical: uniformly accelerated.
questions.example: A ball thrown at an angle traces a parabola.

questions.question: Q18. Derive the range of a projectile R = u²sin2θ/g.
questions.answer: Time of flight T = 2u sinθ/g. Range = horizontal velocity × T = (u cosθ)(2u sinθ/g) = u²(2sinθcosθ)/g = u²sin2θ/g.
questions.shortcut: Range = u cosθ × (2u sinθ/g) → u²sin2θ/g.

questions.question: Q19. At what angle is the range maximum and what is R_max?
questions.answer: R = u²sin2θ/g is maximum when sin2θ = 1, i.e. 2θ = 90°, θ = 45°. Then R_max = u²/g.
questions.shortcut: θ=45° → R_max = u²/g.
questions.example: Same launch speed, 45° gives the farthest range.

questions.question: Q20. Find the maximum height of a projectile launched at 30° with u = 20 m/s.
questions.shortcut: H = u²sin²θ/2g (vertical component).
questions.example: Vertical launch speed u sinθ = 10 m/s → H ≈ 5.1 m.

questions.question: Q21. Find the time of flight for a 45° launch with u = 10 m/s.
questions.answer: T = 2u sinθ/g = 2(10)(0.707)/9.8 ≈ 1.44 s. ▥ 3.5 Projectile Motion  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Projectile Motion: Values at the Apex vs Landing PROFESSOR'S THEORY & VIVA BANK   — the kinds of theory a professor / examiner actually asks
questions.shortcut: T = 2u sinθ/g.
questions.example: The projectile is in the air ≈ 1.44 s.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T1. Derive v² = u² + 2as without using time.
theoryItems.answer: From s = (u+v)t/2 and v = u+at → t=(v−u)/a. Then s = (u+v)(v−u)/2a = (v²−u²)/2a → v²=u²+2as.
theoryItems.example: Used when time is not given.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T2. Derive the time of flight, maximum height and range of a projectile.
theoryItems.answer: T = 2u sinθ/g ; H = u²sin²θ/2g ; R = u²sin2θ/g. From T, use vertical motion (symmetry) for H, and R = horizontal speed × T.
theoryItems.shortcut: Memorize the three; all come from components.

theoryItems.question: [State] T3. Write the four kinematic equations for uniform acceleration.
theoryItems.answer: v=u+at ; s=ut+½at² ; v²=u²+2as ; s=(u+v)t/2. All assume constant a.
theoryItems.shortcut: Pick the one missing the unknown (no time → v²=u²+2as).

theoryItems.question: [Compare] T4. Compare the motion of a body falling vertically with that of a projectile.
theoryItems.answer: Vertical fall: only vertical motion (u=0 downward). Projectile: both horizontal (uniform) and vertical (accelerated) motion. Both have the same vertical acceleration g and the same time-to-reach-the-ground from the same height.
theoryItems.example: From same height, both hit the ground in √(2h/g) time.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T5. Explain the graphical treatment of motion (s-t and v-t graphs).
theoryItems.answer: Slope of s-t = velocity; slope of v-t = acceleration; area under v-t = displacement. A horizontal s-t → rest; curved s-t → acceleration.
theoryItems.shortcut: s-t slope=v; v-t slope=a; area under v-t = s.
theoryItems.example: Constant-velocity v-t gives a rectangle area = vt.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T6. Explain projectile motion as two independent components.
theoryItems.answer: Horizontal: no force → uniform velocity u cosθ. Vertical: gravity → uniformly accelerated u sinθ with g. The combined path is a parabola; time depends only on the vertical motion.
theoryItems.shortcut: Separate x and y; treat independently.
theoryItems.example: Same launch: 30° and 60° give equal ranges.

theoryItems.question: [Why] T7. Why is the trajectory of a projectile a parabola?
theoryItems.answer: Because x ∝ t (constant horizontal speed) and y ∝ t − g t²/2 (accelerated). Eliminating t gives y = x tanθ − gx²/(2u²cos²θ), a quadratic in x → a parabola.
theoryItems.shortcut: y is quadratic in x → parabola.
theoryItems.example: Air resistance would distort it from a parabola.

theoryItems.question: [Viva] T8. Professor: 'Two bodies, one dropped, one fired horizontally from the same height. Which hits first and why?'
theoryItems.answer: Both hit at the same instant, because vertical motion is independent of horizontal motion; both start vertical speed 0 and fall h = ½gt². The horizontal one merely travels further horizontally.

theoryItems.question: [Numerical] T9. A ball is thrown at 20 m/s, 45°. Find range, max height and time of flight.

formulas: Equations (const a): v=u+at; s=ut+½at²; v²=u²+2as; s=(u+v)t/2.
Free fall: u=0, a=g=9.8 m/s². Height of fall h=½gt².
Projectile: range R = u²sin2θ/g (max at θ=45°); H = u²sin²θ/2g; T = 2u sinθ/g.
Graph: slope of s-t = v; area under v-t = s; slope of v-t = a.

▣ 3.1 Instantaneous Velocity & Acceleration
Q1. Define instantaneous velocity.
Answer:  Instantaneous velocity is the velocity at a particular instant, equal to the limit of Δs/Δt as Δt→0, i.e. v = ds/dt.
⚡ Shortcut:  Instantaneous = derivative; average = Δs/Δt.
Example:  Speedometer reading is instantaneous speed.
Q2. Define acceleration. State its SI unit.
Answer:  Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, a = dv/dt. SI unit = m s⁻².
⚡ Shortcut:  a = Δv/Δt (or dv/dt).
Example:  0 to 60 m/s in 20 s → a = 3 m/s².
Q3. Distinguish uniform and non-uniform acceleration.
Answer:  Uniform acceleration: equal change in velocity in equal times (a constant). Non-uniform: change varies with time (a not constant), e.g. a body moving in a circle.
⚡ Shortcut:  constant a → uniform; changing a → non-uniform.
Example:  Free fall = uniform (a=g); car braking = non-uniform.
Q4. Find velocity and acceleration for s = 5t − t² at t = 3 s.
Answer:  v = ds/dt = 5 − 2t → at t=3, v = −1 m/s (1 m/s opposite). a = d²s/dt² = −2 m/s² (constant).
⚡ Shortcut:  v = 1st derivative of s; a = 2nd derivative.
Example:  Negative v means the particle reverses direction.
Q5. What is the significance of the slope of a displacement-time graph?
Answer:  The slope (gradient) of a s–t graph equals velocity. A steeper slope → larger speed; zero slope → body at rest; negative slope → motion opposite to positive direction.
⚡ Shortcut:  slope of s-t = v; slope of v-t = a.
Example:  Horizontal s-t line → body stationary.

▣ 3.2 Relative Velocity
Q6. Define relative velocity of A with respect to B.
Answer:  Relative velocity of A w.r.t. B is V_AB = V_A − V_B, the velocity at which A appears to move when observed from B.
⚡ Shortcut:  V_AB = V_A − V_B (opposite object first minus reference).
Example:  Train A 30 m/s, B 20 m/s same line → A w.r.t. B = 10 m/s.
Q7. Two trains move in opposite directions at 20 m/s and 30 m/s. Find relative speed.
Answer:  Opposite directions → add: relative speed = 20 + 30 = 50 m/s.
⚡ Shortcut:  Same direction → subtract; opposite → add.
Example:  A passenger on the 20 m/s train sees the other at 50 m/s.
Q8. A man walks on a moving train. Express his velocity w.r.t. the ground.
Answer:  If the train's velocity is V and his velocity on the train is u, his ground velocity is V + u (same line, vector sum).
⚡ Shortcut:  Add velocities in same direction; subtract if he walks opposite.
Example:  Train 15 m/s + man 3 m/s forward = 18 m/s w.r.t. ground.
▥ 3.2 Relative Velocity  —  Compare / Contrast Tables
Relative Velocity: Standard Situations
▣ 3.3 Equations of Motion
Q9. Derive v = u + at using a v-t graph.
Answer:  On a v–t graph of uniform acceleration, v = u + (slope)×t, and slope = a. Hence v = u + at.
⚡ Shortcut:  Area under v-t = s; slope = a; final height = u + at.
Example:  u=2, a=3, t=4 → v = 14 m/s.
Q10. A body starts from rest and moves 96 m in 8 s with uniform acceleration. Find a.
Answer:  s = ½at² → 96 = ½·a·64 → a = 3 m/s².
⚡ Shortcut:  From rest: s = ½at², v = at, v² = 2as.
Example:  v = at = 3×8 = 24 m/s.
Q11. Find the stopping distance of a car at 30 m/s with deceleration 5 m/s².
Answer:  v² = u² + 2as, with v=0: 0 = 900 − 2·5·s → s = 90 m.
⚡ Shortcut:  Use v²=u²+2as when time is not given.
Example:  Hence the minimum safe braking distance is 90 m.
Q12. State and derive s = ut + ½at².
Answer:  s = (average velocity)×t = [(u+v)/2]t = [(u+u+at)/2]t = ut + ½at².
⚡ Shortcut:  From v=u+at in average-velocity form.
Example:  u=0,a=2,t=5 → s=25 m.
▥ 3.3 Equations of Motion  —  Compare / Contrast Tables
Equations of Motion: Which One to Use
▣ 3.4 Freely Falling Body
Q13. Define a freely falling body and state its acceleration.
Answer:  A freely falling body is one falling under gravity only, ignoring air resistance. Its acceleration is g ≈ 9.8 m/s² downward, so u=0, a=g.
⚡ Shortcut:  From rest: v = gt, h = ½gt².
Example:  After 2 s, v = 19.6 m/s, h = 19.6 m.
Q14. Time of fall from a 44.1 m height.
Answer:  h = ½gt² → 44.1 = ½(9.8)t² → t² = 9 → t = 3 s.
⚡ Shortcut:  t = √(2h/g).
Example:  A stone dropped from a 44.1 m tower hits the ground in 3 s.
Q15. Why do all bodies fall with the same acceleration in a vacuum?
Answer:  In a vacuum there is no air resistance, so the only force is gravity. Since F=mg and a=F/m=g, the mass cancels and every body has the same acceleration g regardless of mass.
⚡ Shortcut:  In vacuum: a = g for all, mass-independent.
Example:  Feather and coin fall together on the Moon.
Q16. Find the height of a tower if a body takes 4 s to fall from its top.
Answer:  h = ½gt² = ½(9.8)(16) = 78.4 m.
⚡ Shortcut:  h = ½gt².
Example:  Tower ≈ 78.4 m tall.
▥ 3.4 Freely Falling Body  —  Compare / Contrast Tables
Body Thrown Up vs Down from a Height h
▣ 3.5 Projectile Motion
Q17. Define projectile motion and state its assumptions.
Answer:  Projectile motion is the motion of a body thrown into the air under gravity only. Assumptions: neglect air resistance, g constant, motion in a vertical plane, acceleration only vertical.
⚡ Shortcut:  Horizontal: uniform velocity. Vertical: uniformly accelerated.
Example:  A ball thrown at an angle traces a parabola.
Q18. Derive the range of a projectile R = u²sin2θ/g.
Answer:  Time of flight T = 2u sinθ/g. Range = horizontal velocity × T = (u cosθ)(2u sinθ/g) = u²(2sinθcosθ)/g = u²sin2θ/g.
⚡ Shortcut:  Range = u cosθ × (2u sinθ/g) → u²sin2θ/g.
Q19. At what angle is the range maximum and what is R_max?
Answer:  R = u²sin2θ/g is maximum when sin2θ = 1, i.e. 2θ = 90°, θ = 45°. Then R_max = u²/g.
⚡ Shortcut:  θ=45° → R_max = u²/g.
Example:  Same launch speed, 45° gives the farthest range.
Q20. Find the maximum height of a projectile launched at 30° with u = 20 m/s.
⚡ Shortcut:  H = u²sin²θ/2g (vertical component).
Example:  Vertical launch speed u sinθ = 10 m/s → H ≈ 5.1 m.
Q21. Find the time of flight for a 45° launch with u = 10 m/s.
⚡ Shortcut:  T = 2u sinθ/g.
Example:  The projectile is in the air ≈ 1.44 s.
▥ 3.5 Projectile Motion  —  Compare / Contrast Tables
Projectile Motion: Values at the Apex vs Landing
PROFESSOR'S THEORY & VIVA BANK   — the kinds of theory a professor / examiner actually asks
▹ Derive  (derivations & long answers)
[Derive] T1. Derive v² = u² + 2as without using time.
Answer:  From s = (u+v)t/2 and v = u+at → t=(v−u)/a. Then s = (u+v)(v−u)/2a = (v²−u²)/2a → v²=u²+2as.
⚡ Short / exam line:  Eliminate t between two equations.
Example:  Used when time is not given.
[Derive] T2. Derive the time of flight, maximum height and range of a projectile.
Answer:  T = 2u sinθ/g ; H = u²sin²θ/2g ; R = u²sin2θ/g. From T, use vertical motion (symmetry) for H, and R = horizontal speed × T.
⚡ Short / exam line:  Memorize the three; all come from components.
Example:  Max range at 45°: R_max = u²/g.
▹ State  (definitions, laws & formulae)
[State] T3. Write the four kinematic equations for uniform acceleration.
Answer:  v=u+at ; s=ut+½at² ; v²=u²+2as ; s=(u+v)t/2. All assume constant a.
⚡ Short / exam line:  Pick the one missing the unknown (no time → v²=u²+2as).
Example:  0-50 m/s²·3 s → v=15 m/s, s=22.5 m.
▹ Compare  (compare & contrast)
[Compare] T4. Compare the motion of a body falling vertically with that of a projectile.

Answer:  Vertical fall: only vertical motion (u=0 downward). Projectile: both horizontal (uniform) and vertical (accelerated) motion. Both have the same vertical acceleration g and the same time-to-reach-the-ground from the same height.
⚡ Short / exam line:  Vertical = 1D; Projectile = 2D with same g.
Example:  From same height, both hit the ground in √(2h/g) time.
▹ Explain  (working / principle / application)
[Explain] T5. Explain the graphical treatment of motion (s-t and v-t graphs).
Answer:  Slope of s-t = velocity; slope of v-t = acceleration; area under v-t = displacement. A horizontal s-t → rest; curved s-t → acceleration.
⚡ Short / exam line:  s-t slope=v; v-t slope=a; area under v-t = s.
Example:  Constant-velocity v-t gives a rectangle area = vt.
[Explain] T6. Explain projectile motion as two independent components.
Answer:  Horizontal: no force → uniform velocity u cosθ. Vertical: gravity → uniformly accelerated u sinθ with g. The combined path is a parabola; time depends only on the vertical motion.
⚡ Short / exam line:  Separate x and y; treat independently.
Example:  Same launch: 30° and 60° give equal ranges.
▹ Why  (conceptual & 'why' questions)
[Why] T7. Why is the trajectory of a projectile a parabola?
Answer:  Because x ∝ t (constant horizontal speed) and y ∝ t − g t²/2 (accelerated). Eliminating t gives y = x tanθ − gx²/(2u²cos²θ), a quadratic in x → a parabola.
⚡ Short / exam line:  y is quadratic in x → parabola.
Example:  Air resistance would distort it from a parabola.
▹ Viva  (viva-voce probing)
[Viva] T8. Professor: 'Two bodies, one dropped, one fired horizontally from the same height. Which hits first and why?'

Answer:  Both hit at the same instant, because vertical motion is independent of horizontal motion; both start vertical speed 0 and fall h = ½gt². The horizontal one merely travels further horizontally.
⚡ Short / exam line:  Vertical time = √(2h/g) for both.
Example:  Galileo's famous thought experiment.
▹ Numerical  (long numericals / problems)
[Numerical] T9. A ball is thrown at 20 m/s, 45°. Find range, max height and time of flight.
⚡ Short / exam line:  45°: sinθ=cosθ=0.707, sin2θ=1.
Example:  Classic 45° launch.
